subtitle: A curated reading list for people starting out with computer networking.

tldr.problem: People new to the Internet need guidance on what to read to understand TCP/IP networking and internetworking concepts.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1175 provides a categorized bibliography of books, articles, guides, and other resources covering networking topics from basic to advanced.
tldr.outcome: This is an informational guide created by the IETF User Services Working Group to help newcomers find quality learning materials on networking.

today: RFC 1175 is an Informational RFC that documents historical guidance for learning about networking. It has not been obsoleted and remains a historical artifact of early Internet culture and education.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 1175 is a bibliography created by the IETF User Services Working Group. Its purpose is to help newcomers and intermediate users of the Internet find good resources to learn about TCP/IP networking and internetworking concepts. The bibliography collects references to books, journal articles, conference materials, multimedia resources, and RFCs that explain networking at different levels of depth.

The document is aimed at people who are new to the Internet and want to understand how it works, as well as those who support these users. It acts as a starting point for further learning, with each reference including a short abstract explaining what the material covers and how to find it.
sections.plainLanguage: This is like a librarian telling you which Internet books are worth reading and why. It organizes different kinds of learning materials—books, articles, videos—to help you understand networking from the ground up.

sections.title: How the Bibliography Is Organized
sections.content:
RFC 1175 divides learning materials into ten categories to make them easier to find. The categories are: Articles (from magazines and journals), Bibliographies (lists of other references), Books (textbooks and guides), Conferences and Workshops, Glossaries, Guides (practical how-to documents), Multimedia (video and audio materials), Newsletters, Reports and Papers, and Requests for Comments (RFCs).

Within each category, materials are listed alphabetically by author or organization (except RFCs, which are ordered by number). Each entry includes the author, title, publication details, the number of pages, and a short abstract describing the content. The bibliography notes that much of the material is available online and can be downloaded using anonymous FTP, which was the primary file-sharing method at the time.
sections.plainLanguage: The bibliography is organized like a library card catalog, with books, articles, and guides grouped by topic. Each entry tells you what the material covers, who wrote it, and how to get it.

sections.title: Key Recommended Resources
sections.content:
The RFC recommends several materials as especially good starting points. For complete beginners, it suggests reading Ed Krol's "The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Internet" as a gentle introduction. For those wanting to understand Internet protocols in depth, it recommends Charles Hedrick's "Introduction to the Internet Protocols" and Doug Comer's textbook "Internetworking with TCP/IP: Principles, Protocols, and Architecture."

For understanding existing networks and how they connect, the bibliography suggests Tracy L. LaQuey's "Users' Directory of Computer Networks" and John S. Quarterman's "The Matrix: Computer Networks and Conferencing Systems Worldwide." The document encourages readers to scan the entire bibliography to find materials suited to their specific needs and interests.
sections.plainLanguage: The bibliography recommends starting with beginner guides that explain the Internet as a whole, then moving to textbooks that go deeper into how the protocols actually work.

sections.title: How to Find and Obtain Materials
sections.content:
Many of the documents referenced in RFC 1175 are available online through anonymous FTP (File Transfer Protocol), which was the standard way to download files on the early Internet. The RFC includes detailed step-by-step instructions showing how to use the FTP program to connect to computers like nic.ddn.mil and download documents, including how to log in anonymously and navigate directories to find RFC text files.

The bibliography also explains how to submit new entries to the bibliography via email, encouraging others to contribute recommendations for good networking learning materials. The document notes that it is the first version of the "Where to Start" bibliography and welcomes comments and suggested additions to make it more complete and useful.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC explains step-by-step how to download files from the Internet using FTP. It also shows how to suggest new books and articles to add to the reading list.

sections.title: Why This Bibliography Matters
sections.content:
In 1990, when RFC 1175 was published, the Internet was growing rapidly but still unfamiliar to most people. Few structured guides existed to help newcomers learn about networking. This bibliography served a crucial role by collecting and organizing quality learning materials in one place, making it easier for new users and system administrators to find authoritative resources. The categorization and abstracts meant readers could quickly identify materials relevant to their level of expertise and interests.

The document reflects the early Internet culture of peer collaboration, where experienced users documented their knowledge to help others. Although technology has changed, the principle of providing a curated, annotated list of resources remains valuable for anyone learning about networking from the fundamentals up.
sections.plainLanguage: Before the Internet had lots of websites with tutorials, this RFC was like a teacher recommending the best textbooks and articles for learning about how networks actually work.
